Introduces a person, then gives characteristics of their work
Describes how a discovery was made, then explains its importance
The speaker describes attempts or efforts, then acknowledges a limit (poem)
Presents a philosophy or set of principles, then describes a work shaped by it

Describes a problem in research on a topic, then sketches a researcher’s approach to it
Describes a common view, then a recent finding that challenges it
The speaker addresses a criticism of himself, then declares an ambition or commitment (poem)
Presents the regard in which a character is held, then the behaviors that sustain it (literary prose)
Poses a question, then presents a possible answer
Presents someone’s critique, then an attempt to address the problem it identifies
Three moves: introduces a researcher, describes an aspect of the work, explains its significance
Three moves: introduces a project, details its approach, gives a critique it received
Three moves: introduces a phenomenon, rules out two explanations, presents a plausible third
Three moves: explains a finding, generalizes it to a pattern, explains an exception

items.passage: Several of the indigenous writing systems used in West Africa can each be traced to a single inventor. The syllabary devised for the Vai language in present-day Liberia, first documented in the 1830s, is attributed to Momolu Duwalu Bukele. Beginning in 1896, Ibrahim Njoya, king of Bamum in what is now Cameroon, developed a script that changed over the next fourteen years from a collection of pictographic symbols into a syllabary of some eighty characters. In the late 1980s, brothers Ibrahima and Abdoulaye Barry of Guinea invented Adlam, an alphabet for transcribing the Fulani language.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It traces the decline of several West African languages, then describes efforts to preserve them in writing.
It makes a general observation about some writing systems, then gives examples that bear it out.
It identifies the creator of one script, then explains how that script shaped the development of others in the region.
It notes that a region has produced many scripts, then describes how most of those scripts fell out of use.
items.explanation: The first sentence makes a general point: several of West Africa’s indigenous writing systems can each be traced to one inventor. The rest of the text gives three examples: the Vai syllabary, attributed to Bukele; the Bamum script, developed by Njoya; and Adlam, invented by the Barry brothers. So the text makes a general observation and then gives examples that bear it out.

A.recipe: wholly wrong template: decline then preservation (INV)
A.why_wrong: The text never says that any language declined or needed preserving; it reports who invented several scripts.

C.recipe: wholly wrong template built on one example (PART/INV)
C.why_wrong: The text names the inventors of three scripts, not one, and never says that any script shaped the development of the others.

D.why_wrong: The first move is roughly right, but the text never says the scripts fell out of use; it only reports who created them and when.

sources.what: Vai syllabary devised by Momolu Duwalu Bukele; first documented in the 1830s; Vai spoken in present-day Liberia

Bamum script created by Ibrahim Njoya, king of Bamum (now western Cameroon); evolved from pictographic symbols (1896) to a syllabary of 80 characters by 1910; the article gives 80 characters in its lead and 82 plus 10 digits for the 1910 version, hence “some eighty”
Adlam devised by brothers Ibrahima and Abdoulaye Barry in the late 1980s to write Fulani; one of many indigenous scripts developed for specific languages in West Africa
the Barry brothers developed Adlam in Nzérékoré, Guinea, in 1989

items.notes: Subject: humanities (history of writing), replacing the Indigenous loanwords subject (textbook-familiar). Build as in the model: a general situation, then three examples, here each opened by a date or place rather than “For example ... And ...”. The Barry brothers’ ages are left out because sources disagree (one says Abdoulaye was ten). Passage 95 words; official cell median 90 (model 90).

fixes: Vai located as devised “in present-day Liberia” (the language is also spoken in Sierra Leone)
Bamum syllabary given as “some eighty characters” (Wikipedia gives 80 in the lead but 82 plus digits for the 1910 version)
dropped the opening “And” of the last example, which echoed model 1.12

items.rewrite: new subject (West African scripts with known inventors: Vai, Bamum, Adlam) replacing English animal loanwords; options reworded so no two share a prefix and the closing factoid is gone; denser register

items.passage: Navajo textile artist Melissa Cody, who grew up watching her mother and grandmother at the loom and began weaving at age five, works in what is known as the Germantown Revival style. On a traditional Navajo loom built by her father, she weaves tapestries whose vibrant colors, diamond patterns, and overlapping geometric forms seem to rise off the surface in three dimensions. Alongside traditional Navajo symbols, Cody often includes personal tributes and references to pop culture.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a weaving technique developed in the nineteenth century, then traces its gradual abandonment by Navajo weavers.
It compares the work of three generations of weavers in one family, then singles out the youngest as the most inventive.
It presents an artist’s family history, then lists the museums that have exhibited her tapestries.
It introduces a weaver, then describes the distinctive features of the tapestries she creates.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces Melissa Cody, a Navajo textile artist who began weaving as a child, and names the style she works in. The rest of the text describes her tapestries: their colors, patterns, and three-dimensional effect, and the symbols and references she includes in them. So the text introduces a weaver and then describes what is distinctive about her tapestries.

A.recipe: wholly wrong template: technique history then abandonment (INV/REV)
A.why_wrong: The text does not say when the Germantown Revival style arose or that weavers gave it up; Cody works in it today.

B.recipe: wholly wrong template built on the family detail (LIT/STANCE)
B.why_wrong: Cody’s mother and grandmother are mentioned only as the weavers she watched as a child; their work is not compared with hers, and no one is ranked.

C.why_wrong: The family detail fills only part of the first sentence, and the text names no museums; it goes on to describe the tapestries themselves.

sources.what: Navajo textile artist born 1983; grew up watching her mother and grandmother at the loom; began weaving at age 5; Germantown Revival style (vibrant hues, diamond patterns, geometric forms, overlapping lines); traditional Navajo loom built by her father; three-dimensional illusion; Navajo symbols, personal references and pop culture references
works on a traditional Navajo loom; learned to weave at age five from women in her family; weaves personal stories

items.passage: Because the archaea in a sediment core taken from the Arctic seafloor near Loki’s Castle, a hydrothermal vent field, belonged to groups never grown in a laboratory, microbiologists Anja Spang, Thijs Ettema, and colleagues sequenced the DNA extracted directly from the sediment and pieced together genomes from the fragments. One previously unknown lineage, which they named Lokiarchaeota, turned out to be more closely related to eukaryotes, the organisms whose cells contain a nucleus, than any archaea previously known. The finding strongly supports the idea that the eukaryotic cell arose from an archaeal ancestor that already had many of the genes on which eukaryotic complexity depends.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It explains how researchers identified a new group of microbes, then considers what the discovery suggests about the origin of complex cells.
It outlines a method for growing microbes in a laboratory, then describes the organisms that the method allowed researchers to study.
It recounts the collection of a seafloor sample, then explains why the organisms it contained could not be classified.
It reports a discovery made near a hydrothermal vent, then raises doubts about how other scientists have interpreted that discovery.
items.explanation: The first sentence explains how the researchers found the organisms: because the archaea in the Arctic sediment had never been grown in a laboratory, the team sequenced DNA taken straight from the sediment and assembled genomes from it. The second reports the result, a new lineage, Lokiarchaeota, more closely related to eukaryotes than any archaea known before, and the third explains what the finding suggests about the origin of the eukaryotic (complex) cell. So the text explains how a discovery was made and then what it suggests.

B.recipe: wholly wrong template: method for growing microbes (REV)
B.why_wrong: The researchers sequenced DNA from the sediment precisely because these archaea had never been grown in a laboratory; no growing method is described.

C.recipe: later-move break: reversal of the result (REV)
C.why_wrong: The first move is right, but the organisms were classified: the team named a new lineage and showed how it is related to eukaryotes.

D.why_wrong: The text raises no doubts and mentions no other scientists’ interpretations; it says the finding strongly supports a hypothesis about the eukaryotic cell.

sources.what: Spang, Ettema et al. 2015, Nature 521:173: Lokiarchaeota, a new candidate archaeal phylum that forms a monophyletic group with eukaryotes in phylogenomic analyses; genomes encode eukaryotic signature proteins; strong support for the eukaryotic host evolving from an archaeon that already had many components underpinning eukaryote-specific features

gravity core from the Arctic Mid-Ocean Ridge about 15 km from the Loki’s Castle vent field; the archaeal group had never been cultured or sequenced; deep metagenomic sequencing of DNA extracted from the sediment; genome bins assembled from contigs; name refers to Loki’s Castle

items.notes: Subject: natural science (microbiology), replacing Tiktaalik (textbook-famous). “More closely related to eukaryotes than any archaea previously known” restates the paper’s result that Lokiarchaeota and eukaryotes form one monophyletic group in its analyses. Build: how the discovery was made, the result, then its significance, as in 2.2. Passage 105 words; official cell median 82 (model 82); medium maximum 105.
items.rewrite: new subject (Lokiarchaeota found by metagenomic sequencing near Loki’s Castle, Spang and Ettema 2015) replacing Tiktaalik; distractors no longer share the key’s opening words

items.passage:
The following text is from Anne Bradstreet’s 1678 poem “The Author to Her Book.” The speaker addresses a book of her poems, which was printed without her approval, as though it were her child.

Yet being mine own, at length affection would
Thy blemishes amend, if so I could.
I wash’d thy face, but more defects I saw,
And rubbing off a spot, still made a flaw.
I stretcht thy joints to make thee even feet,
Yet still thou run’st more hobbling than is meet.
In better dress to trim thee was my mind,
But nought save home-spun Cloth, i’ th’ house I find.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The speaker lists the faults she sees in a child and then resolves to discipline the child more strictly.
The speaker regrets having allowed her book to be printed and then promises to revise it before it is printed again.
The speaker recounts her efforts to improve something she has made and then acknowledges a limit on what she can do.
The speaker praises the simple materials available in her home and then contrasts them with the finery she once owned.
items.explanation: In the first six lines the speaker tries to improve her book, which she treats as a child: she washes its face, rubs at a spot, and stretches its joints, though each attempt leaves a flaw. In the last two lines she says she meant to dress it better but finds nothing in the house except “home-spun Cloth.” So she recounts her efforts to improve what she has made and then acknowledges a limit on what she can do.

A.why_wrong: The “child” is a figure for the book, and the speaker is trying to mend its flaws, not resolving to discipline anyone.

B.recipe: contradicts the context line and misreads the tense (REV/INV)
B.why_wrong: The book was printed without her approval, so she did not allow it, and the excerpt describes revisions she has already attempted, not a promise about a later printing.

D.why_wrong: The speaker does not praise her plain cloth; she wanted “better dress” and has only home-spun cloth to use. No finery she once owned is mentioned.

sources.what: text of lines 11–18, from Several Poems, 2nd ed. (Boston: John Foster, 1678)
1678 Several Poems published posthumously in Boston; poem’s background (manuscript taken to the printer by her brother-in-law)
same text in the 1891 Campbell edition (original spelling)

items.notes: Literature (poem, public domain, published 1678). Lines 11–18 copied exactly from the RPO text (Several Poems, 1678), straight apostrophes made curly. Neither Bradstreet nor this poem appears in any official transcript. Official cell median 50 words (model 50).
items.rewrite: options rewritten: distractors no longer mirror the Gilman item’s choices or share the key’s opening, key reworded (recounts efforts to improve, acknowledges a limit); excerpt unchanged

items.passage: Italian-born Brazilian architect Lina Bo Bardi championed what she called “poor architecture,” meaning not poverty but the pursuit of maximum dignity and communication through minimal, humble means rather than costly materials or ornament. Her SESC Pompéia, a leisure center in São Paulo completed in stages between 1977 and 1986, exemplifies that approach. Rather than demolish the disused steel-drum factory on the site, Bo Bardi stripped away its plaster to expose the rough concrete beneath, preserved the sheds where neighborhood residents were already playing soccer and staging plays, and beside them raised new concrete towers joined by aerial walkways.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a dispute over whether an old factory should be preserved, then explains how that dispute was settled.
It summarizes an architect’s career, then argues that her later buildings were less inventive than her earlier ones.
It sets out an architect’s guiding principle, then recounts the objections critics raised to a building based on it.
It introduces an idea about what architecture should aim for, then discusses a project that embodies that idea.
items.explanation: The first sentence presents Bo Bardi’s idea of “poor architecture”: seeking dignity and communication through humble means rather than costly materials. The rest of the text describes SESC Pompéia, which the text says exemplifies that idea: she kept and exposed the old factory, kept the uses residents had already given it, and added new concrete towers. So the text introduces an idea about architecture and then discusses a project that embodies it.

A.recipe: wholly wrong template built on the factory (LIT/INV)
A.why_wrong: The text reports Bo Bardi’s choice to keep the factory but no dispute about whether to preserve it.

B.recipe: wholly wrong template: career survey plus judgment (INV/STANCE)
B.why_wrong: The text discusses one idea and one project; it does not survey her career or compare her earlier and later buildings.

C.why_wrong: The first move is right, but the text says nothing about critics or objections; it describes how the building puts the idea into practice.

sources.what: Italian-born Brazilian architect; “Poor Architecture”, divorced from pretentiousness; SESC Pompéia, a former steel drum and refrigerator factory in São Paulo turned leisure center, completed in stages 1977–1986; locals already used the site for football, dance and theater and she kept those uses; old plaster stripped and sandblasted to reveal rough concrete; new concrete towers linked by aerial walkways
her 1986 essay on the Pompéia drum works; architettura povera in the artisanal sense, maximum communication and dignity with minimal and humble means
a pair of new concrete towers housing sports facilities, connected to each other by eight pedestrian walkways; conversion 1977 to 1986; soccer teams and a theater company had occupied the building

items.notes: Subject: arts (architecture), replacing Dogme 95. Idea and work are both Bo Bardi’s, unlike the model, where one writer’s idea shapes another’s book. Passage 97 words; official cell median 95 (model 95).

fixes: the aerial walkways join the two new towers to each other, not the old sheds to the towers (SESC Pompeia article); passage now says she raised new towers beside the sheds, joined by walkways

items.rewrite: new subject (Lina Bo Bardi’s “poor architecture” and SESC Pompéia) replacing Dogme 95; key reworded away from the model’s “philosophy ... work shaped by that philosophy”

items.passage: Citizen science projects such as eBird, to which birdwatchers submit lists of the species they see, and NestWatch, in which volunteers record how many eggs are laid and hatched in active nests, enlist members of the public to gather data for scientific research. Both are what researchers call contributory projects: scientists design the study, and participants mainly supply observations. In co-created projects, by contrast, scientists and members of the public design the study together, and at least some participants take part in most or all stages of the research, from posing questions to interpreting and sharing results.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes two research projects that rely on volunteers, then explains why one has attracted more participants than the other.
It characterizes a kind of research by citing two projects, then describes a category of such research in which the public’s role is broader.
It presents two examples of citizen science, then argues that projects designed by scientists yield more reliable data than those designed with the public.
It traces the history of public participation in science, then proposes a new way of recruiting volunteers.
items.explanation: The first sentence characterizes citizen science by citing two projects, eBird and NestWatch, in which volunteers collect data for research, and the second classifies them as contributory projects, which scientists design. The last sentence describes co-created projects, in which members of the public help design the study and may take part in every stage. So the text characterizes a kind of research through two examples and then describes a category of it in which the public does more.

A.recipe: wholly wrong template: comparison of popularity (INV)
A.why_wrong: The text never compares how many people take part in eBird and NestWatch; both serve as examples of the same kind of project.

C.why_wrong: The first move is right, but the text makes no claim about which kind of project yields more reliable data; it only describes how the public’s role differs.

D.recipe: wholly wrong template: history then proposal (INV)
D.why_wrong: The text gives no history of public participation and proposes nothing; it describes two existing kinds of project.

sources.what: models from Bonney et al. 2009: contributory projects are generally designed by scientists and the public primarily contributes data; co-created projects are designed by scientists and members of the public together, with at least some participants involved in most or all aspects of the research; NestWatch given as a contributory project
NestWatch: volunteers record when nesting begins, how many eggs are laid and hatch, and how many young survive
eBird, launched 2002 by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and National Audubon Society; participants submit observations as checklists
eBird described as a contributory citizen science project

items.notes: Subject: social science (research participation), replacing map projections. Same moves as 2.11 (a field shown through two examples, then a subset that goes further) in a different architecture: the second sentence labels the examples, the third contrasts a broader kind. The “impossible to be useful” style distractor is gone. Passage 97 words; official cell median 91 (model 91).

items.passage: The open ocean may harbor as many as a million undescribed species, but many of its inhabitants, among them jellyfish and squid, are soft-bodied, and the underwater equipment available for collecting them, much of it designed for the rough work of ocean mining and construction, frequently damages or destroys such animals before they can be studied. Zhi Ern Teoh and colleagues at Harvard University’s Wyss Institute addressed this difficulty with the rotary-actuated dodecahedron (RAD) sampler: driven by a single motor, its five 3D-printed petals fold into a hollow, twelve-sided enclosure that gently surrounds an organism and can reopen to release it unharmed.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It presents a common belief about ocean life, then describes an expedition that disproved that belief.
It identifies an obstacle to studying certain sea creatures, then concludes that the obstacle is unlikely to be overcome soon.
It describes a difficulty in collecting some marine animals, then outlines a device designed to overcome that difficulty.
It explains how a sampling device was invented, then reports the new species that researchers discovered with it.
items.explanation: The first sentence describes the difficulty: many ocean animals, such as jellyfish and squid, are soft-bodied, and existing collecting equipment often damages or destroys them. The second describes the RAD sampler, a folding device that encloses an animal gently and can release it unharmed. So the text describes a difficulty in collecting some marine animals and then outlines a device designed to overcome it.

A.recipe: wholly wrong template: belief then disproof (INV)
A.why_wrong: No belief about ocean life is disproved and no expedition is described; the text concerns a collecting problem and a device.

B.why_wrong: The first move is right, but the text does not suggest that the obstacle will persist; it describes a device that addresses it.

D.why_wrong: The text describes the device but reports no new species found with it, and it opens with the problem the device was built to solve.

sources.what: open ocean may hold up to a million undescribed species; many soft-bodied (jellyfish, squid, octopuses) and damaged or destroyed by existing tools largely designed for ocean mining and construction; RAD sampler by first author Zhi Ern Teoh (Wyss Institute, lab of Robert Wood); five 3D-printed petals folded by a single motor into a hollow dodecahedron; captures and releases animals without harm; mounted on an ROV
Teoh et al. 2018, Science Robotics: rotary-actuated folding polyhedra to noninvasively enclose delicate midwater organisms; single rotary actuator; field-tested on ROVs

items.notes: Subject: natural science and engineering, replacing Ginzburg’s The Cheese and the Worms (too close to the model’s historian and source problem). Two long sentences, problem then approach, as in 2.16. Passage 102 words; official cell median 91 (model 91).
items.rewrite: new subject (RAD sampler for soft-bodied ocean animals, Teoh and colleagues 2018) replacing the Ginzburg history item; the copied “set evidence aside” distractor replaced

items.passage: Modern crocodilians and birds, the closest living relatives of non-avian dinosaurs, lay hard-shelled eggs, and paleontologists long assumed on that basis that non-avian dinosaurs did as well. A 2020 study led by Mark Norell of the American Museum of Natural History suggests otherwise. Chemical and microscopic analyses of unusually well-preserved eggs of Protoceratops, from Mongolia, and Mussaurus, from Argentina, showed that their shells had originally been soft, and comparisons with the eggshells of other reptiles indicated that the first dinosaurs laid soft eggs, with hard shells evolving independently at least three times.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It explains the basis for a long-held assumption, then reports research that calls that assumption into question.
It describes how fossil eggs are usually dated, then explains why a newer dating technique is more reliable.
It presents a recent finding about dinosaur eggs, then describes the earlier research on which that finding was built.
It notes a disagreement between two teams of paleontologists, then explains how a new analysis settled it.
items.explanation: The first sentence gives a long-held assumption and its basis: crocodilians and birds lay hard-shelled eggs, so paleontologists assumed non-avian dinosaurs did too. The rest of the text reports a 2020 study suggesting otherwise: the eggs of Protoceratops and Mussaurus were originally soft, and the first dinosaurs probably laid soft eggs. So the text explains the basis for an assumption and then reports research that calls it into question.

B.recipe: wholly wrong template: method then better method (INV)
B.why_wrong: The text says nothing about dating fossil eggs; the analyses it mentions concern what the shells were made of.

C.why_wrong: The text begins with the older assumption, not the recent finding, and the 2020 study contradicts that assumption rather than building on earlier research.

D.recipe: wholly wrong template: disagreement then resolution (INV)
D.why_wrong: Only one research team is mentioned, and the text describes an assumption being challenged, not a disagreement being settled.

sources.what: Norell et al. 2020, Nature 583:406: since crocodilians and birds lay hard-shelled eggs, that type was inferred for non-avian dinosaurs; mineralogical, organochemical and ultrastructural evidence that Protoceratops and Mussaurus eggs were originally soft-shelled; ancestral-state reconstruction with other diapsid eggshells shows the first dinosaur egg was soft; hard shells evolved independently at least three times
study led by Mark Norell of the American Museum of Natural History; Protoceratops eggs from Mongolia, Mussaurus eggs from Argentina

items.notes: Subject: natural science (paleontology), replacing female birdsong (the judge flagged the frame and a challenges/confirms mirror pair). No option now mirrors another. Passage 89 words; official cell median 74 (model 74).
items.rewrite: new subject (soft-shelled first dinosaur eggs, Norell 2020) replacing female songbird song; removed the challenges/confirms mirror pair; denser register

items.passage:
The following text is from John Keats’s 1817 poem “Sleep and Poetry.” Just before this passage, the speaker describes the kind of poetry he hopes will flourish.

Will not some say that I presumptuously
Have spoken? that from hastening disgrace
’T were better far to hide my foolish face?
That whining boyhood should with reverence bow
Ere the dread thunderbolt could reach [me]? How!
If I do hide myself, it sure shall be
In the very fane [temple], the light of Poesy:
If I do fall, at least I will be laid
Beneath the silence of a poplar shade;
And over me the grass shall be smooth shaven;
And there shall be a kind memorial graven.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The speaker scorns critics who have attacked his poems and then predicts that he will soon be famous.
The speaker anticipates an objection to his ambitions and then vows to remain faithful to poetry whatever happens.
The speaker confesses that his early verses were foolish and then resolves to give up writing in favor of a quieter life.
The speaker describes the funeral of a poet he admired and then reflects on how the dead should be honored.
items.explanation: In the first five lines the speaker imagines what some people will say: that he has spoken presumptuously and should hide his face. After “How!” he replies that if he hides, it will be in “the light of Poesy,” and if he fails, he will at least lie beneath a poplar with a memorial. So he anticipates an objection and then vows to stay devoted to poetry whatever happens.

A.why_wrong: The criticism is one the speaker imagines (“Will not some say”), not an attack he has received, and he predicts no fame; he even allows that he may “fall.”

C.why_wrong: “Foolish face” is the critics’ imagined charge, not his own confession, and he rejects their advice to hide, insisting he will stay in “the light of Poesy.”

D.why_wrong: The grave and memorial are the speaker’s own, imagined in case he fails; no funeral or other poet appears.

poem published in Keats’s Poems (1817)
“Sleep and Poetry” is a poem by John Keats

items.passage:
The following text is from Henry James’s 1880 novel Washington Square. Dr. Austin Sloper is a physician who practices in New York City during the first half of the nineteenth century.

It was an element in Dr. Sloper’s reputation that his learning and his skill were very evenly balanced; he was what you might call a scholarly doctor, and yet there was nothing abstract in his remedies—he always ordered you to take something. Though [Dr. Sloper] was felt to be extremely thorough, he was not uncomfortably theoretic, and if he sometimes explained matters rather more minutely than might seem of use to the patient, he never went so far (like some practitioners one has heard of) as to trust to the explanation alone, but always left behind him an inscrutable prescription.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It recounts how a physician acquired his medical training and then explains why patients found his prescriptions hard to follow.
It argues that a doctor relied too heavily on theory and then gives examples of patients harmed by that reliance.
It describes the reputation of physicians in general and then presents one doctor as an exception to it.
It names a quality for which a doctor is esteemed and then details how his treatment of patients displays that quality.
items.explanation: The first clause names a quality behind Dr. Sloper’s reputation: his learning and his skill were evenly balanced. The rest of the text shows that balance in how he treats patients: he is thorough and sometimes explains at length, but he never relies on explanation alone and always leaves a prescription. So the text names a quality for which he is esteemed and then details how his treatment of patients displays it.

A.why_wrong: The text says nothing about his training, and “inscrutable” describes the prescription itself; nothing suggests that patients could not follow it.

B.why_wrong: The text says he was “not uncomfortably theoretic” and never trusted explanation alone, and it names no patient who was harmed.

C.why_wrong: The text is about Dr. Sloper’s own reputation from the start; other practitioners appear only in a brief aside.

sources.what: text from chapter 1 (Macmillan edition)
Washington Square written and published in 1880 by Henry James
the doctor’s full name, Austin Sloper (chapter 1)

Two sentences copied exactly from Gutenberg #2870; one CB-style substitution, “he” replaced by “[Dr. Sloper]” at the start of the second sentence. Henry James appears in no official transcript; the full official bank (cb_api) has two items from his The Portrait of a Lady (words_in_context 3bd32343, transitions feb1e6da), a different work. Model 2.22 is 129 words with its source line; this passage is 131 (100 in the excerpt).

items.passage: How do Saharan silver ants (Cataglyphis bombycina) forage in the full midday sun, when the desert surface can reach 70°C, while keeping their bodies below a critical thermal maximum of 53.6°C? Norman Nan Shi, Nanfang Yu, and their colleagues suggest that the answer lies in the dense coat of hairs that gives the ants their silvery sheen. Examining the hairs by electron microscopy, the team found that their triangular cross-sections make them highly reflective of the visible and near-infrared light in which sunlight is concentrated while also enhancing the ants’ emission of mid-infrared radiation, which lets them shed excess body heat toward the cooler sky.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The text describes how an insect searches for food, then explains why its searches are most successful at midday.
The text raises a question about an insect, then reports that researchers have not been able to agree on an answer.
The text asks how an animal tolerates extreme heat, then presents research that offers an explanation.
The text presents a hypothesis about an insect’s coloring, then describes an experiment showing that the hypothesis was mistaken.
items.explanation: The text opens with a question: how can Saharan silver ants forage in the midday heat while keeping their bodies below a dangerous temperature? It then reports research suggesting an answer: the ants’ triangular hairs reflect sunlight and help the ants radiate heat away. So the text asks how an animal tolerates extreme heat and then presents research offering an explanation.

A.why_wrong: The text mentions midday foraging only to show how hot the ants’ conditions are; it does not describe how they find food or say why midday searches succeed.

B.why_wrong: The first move is right, but the text reports one team’s suggested answer and no disagreement among researchers.

D.why_wrong: The study’s findings support the idea that the hairs keep the ants cool; nothing in the text is shown to be mistaken.

sources.what: Shi, Tsai, Camino, Bernard, Yu and Wehner 2015, Science 349:298: silvery appearance created by a dense array of triangular hairs that enhance reflectivity in the visible and near-infrared, where solar radiation culminates, and emissivity in the mid-infrared, letting the ants dissipate heat
ants forage in the full midday sun when surface temperatures reach up to 70°C and must keep their body temperature below a critical thermal maximum of 53.6°C
electron microscopy of hairs with triangular cross-sections (Norman Nan Shi and Nanfang Yu, Columbia); mid-infrared emission lets the body exchange heat with the cooler sky

items.passage: Swedish traffic safety researcher Astrid Linder has criticized vehicle safety regulations for assessing occupant protection with crash test dummies based on an average-sized man, a figure whose stature and mass correspond to those of a woman larger than roughly 90 percent of women. Seats engineered around such dummies, Linder and her colleagues argue, protect women less effectively against whiplash, an injury for which women’s risk is up to three times that of men even in comparable collisions. As coordinator of ADSEAT, a European research project, Linder oversaw the development of EvaRID, a computational dummy representing an average-sized woman in rear-impact tests.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It traces the history of a vehicle safety regulation, then argues that the regulation has done more to protect women than men.
It reports a researcher’s concern about a type of testing equipment, then explains why manufacturers have resisted replacing that equipment.
It describes a shortcoming that a researcher has identified in how vehicles are tested, then presents an effort she led to remedy it.
It identifies a difference in how often women and men are injured in collisions, then attributes that difference to the way each group drives.
items.explanation: The first two sentences present Linder’s critique: safety regulations assess seats with dummies based on an average-sized man, and seats built around such dummies protect women less well against whiplash. The last sentence gives an example of her attempt to address the problem: under her coordination, the ADSEAT project developed EvaRID, a computational dummy representing an average-sized woman. So the text describes a shortcoming she identified and then an effort she led to remedy it.

A.why_wrong: The text gives no history of a regulation, and it says current testing protects women less effectively, not more.

B.why_wrong: The first move is right, but no manufacturers or their reactions are mentioned; the text goes on to describe a new dummy that Linder’s project developed.

D.why_wrong: Women’s higher whiplash risk supports Linder’s critique, but the text never attributes it to driving; it links the problem to how seats are designed and tested.

sources.what: Linder and Svedberg 2019, Accident Analysis and Prevention 127: in European regulatory tests the average-sized male represents the adult population and the average-sized female has been excluded

EvaRID paper (Chang, ..., Linder 2010): female whiplash risk 1.5 to 3 times the male risk even in similar crashes; the 50th percentile male dummy corresponds to a 90th–95th percentile female in stature and mass; seats and whiplash protection adapted to the male and more effective for males; EvaRID, a computational model of an average female, developed in ADSEAT
Astrid Linder, ADSEAT project coordinator at VTI; EvaRID, a virtual crash test dummy representing an average woman
ADSEAT summary paper (Linder et al. 2013): finite element model EvaRID of an average female

items.passage: Musicologist Eileen Southern, whose doctoral research concerned Renaissance music, became in the 1970s the first Black woman appointed a tenured full professor at Harvard University. Her book The Music of Black Americans: A History (1971), written partly in response to a colleague’s dismissive question about whether Black music comprised anything besides jazz, surveyed the full gamut of genres to which African Americans had contributed over some 450 years. Although earlier writers had interpreted individual aspects of that music, Southern’s history was the first comprehensive scholarly treatment of the subject, and it opened a vast new area of academic inquiry.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It introduces a distinguished scholar, describes one of her major works, and then explains why that work proved so consequential.
It presents a musicologist’s early training, summarizes a book she wrote on Renaissance music, and then reports how colleagues responded to it.
It identifies a pioneering academic, recounts the remark that prompted one of her books, and then suggests that such remarks were common at her university.
It mentions a professor’s appointment at a university, outlines the courses she taught there, and then lists the honors she received.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces Eileen Southern, a musicologist who became the first Black woman appointed a tenured full professor at Harvard. The second describes her book The Music of Black Americans, and the third explains its significance: it was the first comprehensive scholarly treatment of its subject and opened a new area of academic inquiry. So the text introduces a distinguished scholar, describes one of her major works, and then explains why that work mattered.

B.why_wrong: Renaissance music was the subject of her doctoral research, not of the book the text describes, and no colleagues’ responses to a book are reported; the last sentence explains the book’s significance.

C.why_wrong: The first two moves are roughly right, but the text does not suggest that such remarks were common at her university or say where the colleague worked.

D.recipe: wholly wrong template built on the appointment (PART/INV)
D.why_wrong: The appointment only introduces Southern; the text describes no courses and lists no honors.

sources.what: doctoral dissertation on Renaissance music (NYU 1961); first Black woman to become a tenured full professor at Harvard (1970s); a colleague’s question “Black music? Besides jazz, what is there?” partly prompted The Music of Black Americans, which covers the full gamut of genres to which African Americans contributed over 450 years

Harvard memorial minute: The Music of Black Americans: A History (1971) was the first thoroughgoing scholarly treatment of the subject, though earlier authors had interpreted individual aspects, essentially revealing a vast new area of academic inquiry
book published 1971; tenured full professor at Harvard in the 1970s

items.passage: Never Alone (Kisima Inŋitchuŋa), a 2014 puzzle-platform video game, was developed by Upper One Games, a company owned by the Cook Inlet Tribal Council, in partnership with some forty Alaska Native elders, storytellers, and community members. Adapting the traditional Iñupiaq tale “Kunuuksaayuka,” the game alternates control between a girl named Nuna and an Arctic fox and, as players progress, unlocks “cultural insights”: short documentary videos in which Iñupiat elders and storytellers share their stories. Reviewing the game for GameSpot, Daniel Hindes credited those videos with supplying valuable cultural context but faulted its sluggish, imprecise controls.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It introduces a video game made with an Indigenous community, explains how the game adapts a traditional story, and then describes plans for a sequel.
It describes the founding of a game company, summarizes several stories told by Iñupiat elders, and then evaluates which story best suits a video game.
It presents a collaborative game project, details features that set the game apart, and then explains why critics agreed those features were successful.
It introduces a game and the partnership that produced it, describes how the game was designed, and then reports one reviewer’s mixed assessment of the game.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces Never Alone and the partnership with Alaska Native elders, storytellers, and community members that produced it. The second describes the game’s design: it adapts an Iñupiaq tale, alternates between a girl and a fox, and unlocks short documentary videos. The third reports a GameSpot reviewer’s response, which praised the videos but criticized the controls. So the text introduces a game, describes its design, and then reports one reviewer’s mixed assessment.

A.why_wrong: The first two moves are right, but the text never mentions a sequel; it ends with a review of the game.

B.why_wrong: The company is named but its founding is not described, only one traditional tale is mentioned, and the text does not weigh stories against one another.

C.why_wrong: The first two moves are right, but the text reports one reviewer, not agreement among critics, and his judgment was mixed: he faulted the controls.

sources.what: 2014 puzzle-platform game developed by Upper One Games (the Cook Inlet Tribal Council’s for-profit company); about 40 Alaska Native elders, storytellers and community members; based on the Iñupiaq tale “Kunuuksaayuka”; player swaps between Nuna and an Arctic fox; collectible “cultural insights”, short videos of Iñupiaq elders, storytellers and community members sharing their stories

Daniel Hindes’s GameSpot review (February 2015): videos unlocked as you progress “do an excellent job of giving a cultural context”; “sluggish controls that require a precision they are not capable of providing”

items.passage: In May 2015, more than 200,000 saiga antelopes, over 60 percent of the species’ global population, died within three weeks in central Kazakhstan, killed by hemorrhagic septicemia caused by the bacterium Pasteurella multocida. A contagion passed from animal to animal is an improbable cause, since entire calving aggregations sickened almost simultaneously. Nor was the pathogen a recent arrival: nearly identical strains have long persisted in apparently healthy saigas. More plausible is the account of Richard Kock of the Royal Veterinary College and colleagues, who link the event to unusually high humidity and heat, conditions associated with outbreaks of the disease in other animals.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a mass die-off of animals, dismisses two proposed causes of it, and then concludes that its true cause will probably never be known.
It reports a catastrophic event, discounts two possible explanations of it, and then identifies a cause that the author considers more likely.
It presents a sudden loss of wildlife, discusses two explanations that the author finds equally persuasive, and then describes research that combines them.
It recounts an event that devastated a species, rules out two explanations for the event, and then explains how the species has since recovered.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces the event: the death of more than 200,000 saigas from hemorrhagic septicemia in 2015. The next two sentences discount two explanations: a contagion passed between animals (whole herds fell ill almost at once) and a newly arrived pathogen (similar strains live in healthy saigas). The last sentence presents the account the author calls “more plausible”: unusually high humidity and heat. So the text reports an event, discounts two explanations, and identifies a cause the author considers more likely.

A.recipe: later-move break: reversal of the conclusion (REV)
A.why_wrong: The first two moves are right, but the text ends by favoring an explanation, not by saying the cause will never be known.

C.why_wrong: The author argues against the first two explanations (“an improbable cause,” “Nor was”) rather than finding them persuasive, and no research combining them is described.

D.why_wrong: The first two moves are right, but the text says nothing about the species recovering; its last sentence offers a cause of the die-off.

sources.what: Kock et al. 2018 (first and corresponding author Richard A. Kock, Royal Veterinary College, London), Science Advances 4:eaao2314: more than 200,000 saigas died in 3 weeks in central Kazakhstan in May 2015, about 62% of the global population; cause hemorrhagic septicemia from Pasteurella multocida type B; temporal and spatial distribution made horizontal transmission of a contagion unlikely; near-simultaneous onset within and between large groups; near-identical strains found for decades in apparently healthy saigas (latent endemic infection); unusually high humidity and temperature before the event; P. multocida linked to humidity and heat in other species

items.passage: Searching Kepler data for additional planets close to hot Jupiters, gas giants that orbit their stars in a few days, Jason Steffen and colleagues found no sign of any, an absence readily explained if, as many astronomers think, such planets reach their orbits through high-eccentricity migration, an inward passage along a highly elongated path that would destabilize or engulf smaller neighbors. Later analyses confirmed that hot Jupiters almost never have close companions. WASP-47b, flanked by a super-Earth and a Neptune-sized planet, is a striking exception, which Chelsea Huang, Yanqin Wu, and Amaury Triaud attribute to its having formed near its present orbit, without such migration.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It reports an observation and a probable reason for it, indicates that the observation holds broadly, and then presents an exception along with the likely cause of that exception.
It describes an unsuccessful search for planets around distant stars, proposes improvements to the method used, and then reports a discovery made with the improved method.

It presents a result from a planetary survey and an account of that result, notes that later studies confirmed it, and then describes a system that its discoverers regard as evidence against that account.
It summarizes a finding about giant planets along with an explanation, reports that later analyses failed to reproduce the finding, and then identifies a flaw in the original study.
items.explanation: The first sentence reports Steffen and colleagues’ observation that no other planets showed up close to hot Jupiters and explains it: migration along a highly elongated path would destroy such neighbors. The second says later analyses found that hot Jupiters almost never have close companions. The third presents WASP-47b as an exception and gives its likely cause: it probably formed near its present orbit without migrating. So the text reports and explains an observation, extends it to a broader group, and then presents and accounts for an exception.

B.why_wrong: The search did come up empty, but the text proposes no better method, and WASP-47b is presented as an exception explained by how it formed, not as a discovery made with an improved method.

C.recipe: later-move break: stance flip and misattribution (STANCE/SWAP)
C.why_wrong: The first two moves are right, but the text does not treat WASP-47b as evidence against the migration account: Huang, Wu, and Triaud explain its neighbors by its having formed without that migration, which is what the account predicts. The text also never says they discovered the system.

D.recipe: later-move break: reversal of the second move (REV/INV)
D.why_wrong: Later analyses confirmed the observation rather than failing to reproduce it, and no flaw in the original study is identified.

sources.what: Steffen et al. 2012, PNAS 109:7982: Kepler search for companions near hot Jupiter candidates (periods near 3 days) found no transits and no transit timing variations

Huang, Wu and Triaud 2016, ApJ 825:98: hot Jupiters, with the singular exception of WASP-47b, have no detectable inner or outer companions; WASP-47b likely formed in situ; dynamical migration destroys inner systems; hot Jupiters defined by periods inward of 10 days

Mustill, Davies and Johansen 2015: highly eccentric giant planets that become hot Jupiters clear out low-mass inner planets, explaining the observed lack of companions; supports most hot Jupiters reaching their orbits after a high-eccentricity phase
Becker et al. 2015: WASP-47 hosts a hot Jupiter, a Neptune-sized outer planet and a super-Earth inner companion
